text: The Honda Juno is a scooter that came in two versions: the K-series produced in 1954 (K, KA, KB) and the M-series introduced in 1962 (M80, M85). The Juno K, Honda's first scooter, was launched in 1954 as a deliberately sophisticated model, designed to compete with established scooters like the Fuji Rabbit and Mitsubishi Silver Pigeon. It featured the first electric start, a full windscreen with a tilt-back sun-shade, and built-in signal lamps, and introduced Fibre-Reinforced Plastic (FRP) body construction to Japan. Only 5,980 units were produced over a period of one and a half years. Kihachiro Kawashima, who retired as executive vice-president in 1979, recalled the Juno K as a "splendid failure" due to its high cost, engine overheating, heavier-than-expected FRP body that made it underpowered and clumsy, problematic cantilevered suspension, and customer dissatisfaction with the motorcycle-style clutch operation. The final Juno KB model is identifiable by enlarged rear vents and new vents on the windscreen. Technologies from the Juno K, including the electric start, were later used in the 1957 C71 Dream, and the Plastics department led by Shozo Tsuchida developed polyethylene components that became key in the Super Cub. The Juno M80/M85, introduced in November 1961, took a different design approach: it lacked an upper windscreen, used an exposed horizontal-twin engine instead of an enclosed fan-cooled unit, and featured conventional monocoque steel body construction rather than FRP panels over tube. It also introduced a clutchless Badalini-type hydraulic-mechanical transmission, which later influenced the development of Hondamatic motorcycle transmissions. The M80 and M85 are essentially identical, with the M85 designation denoting a mid-year engine enlargement. The Juno line was discontinued by year-end, with only 5,880 units produced in total.
